name: Pig collagen

angle.text: Pig collagen appears in Korean sheet masks and creams for plumper, smoother skin, and is also taken as a supplement. Porcine collagen has real surgical uses, but cosmetic trials are lacking.

summary: A K-beauty mask protein with real surgical uses but no cosmetic trials, and a skin-penetration question the encyclopedia answers negatively.
note: Wikipedia says intact collagen does not penetrate skin.
currentQuick:
Pig collagen is collagen from porcine skin, used in some Korean sheet masks and creams, and separately in medical dressings and membranes.
No studies were found on masks improving appearance, and Wikipedia reports no clinical evidence for topical or oral collagen against wrinkles as of 2025.
How it works: Marketing holds that collagen hydrates or firms skin; Wikipedia notes intact collagen is too large to enter skin, so cosmetics often use hydrolysed peptides.
Risks and caveats: As an animal-derived product it may matter to people avoiding pork; porcine tissue has triggered immune responses in transplant research. No cosmetic safety data were found.
deepLead:
Pig (porcine) collagen is collagen protein derived from pig skin or connective tissue. In beauty it appears in sheet masks and creams, particularly in Korean products, and as a supplement; in medicine, porcine collagen is used in wound dressings and dental and surgical membranes.
Wikipedia states that intact collagen is too large to penetrate skin when applied topically, that cosmetics therefore often use hydrolysed forms, and that as of 2025 no clinical evidence supports oral or topical collagen products for wrinkles or skin ageing. Proponents of collagen products hold that they hydrate or firm skin.

name: Tea tree extract

angle.text: Tea tree oil and extract are used in cleansers and spot treatments by people targeting acne and blemishes. The oil has limited acne trial evidence, while the extract has almost none.

summary: An Australian antibacterial botanical common in acne products; the oil has limited acne evidence, the extract has almost none.
note: Oil is toxic if swallowed and can cause skin allergy.
currentQuick:
Tea tree extract and oil come from an Australian shrub and are common in acne and blemish products for their antibacterial reputation.
A Cochrane review summarised on Wikipedia found one low-quality acne trial favouring the oil. Trials specific to the extract were not found.
How it works: The oil's main component is terpinen-4-ol, which has antimicrobial activity in lab tests.
Risks and caveats: Skin irritation and allergy occur, especially with oxidised oil. Swallowing is highly toxic, and a possible link to breast enlargement has been reported.
deepLead:
Tea tree extract and tea tree oil derive from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, a plant native to eastern Australia. The oil is promoted for acne, dandruff and minor skin infections, and tea tree extract appears in cleansers and blemish products.
The published evidence is mostly for the oil rather than extracts. A 2015 Cochrane review, as summarised on Wikipedia, found one low-quality trial showing benefit for acne lesions. Wikipedia also reports skin irritation and allergy, toxicity if swallowed, and a possible link to breast enlargement in boys and men.

name: Acerola fruit extract

angle.text: Acerola extract is included in beauty supplements as a natural vitamin C source, taken for brighter, firmer skin. Skin evidence exists only for multi-ingredient blends, not for the extract on its own.

summary: Vitamin-C-rich tropical fruit extract used in beauty supplements; skin evidence exists only for multi-ingredient blends.
note: Published skin data come from a blended product, not acerola alone.
currentQuick:
Acerola extract comes from a tropical fruit that is one of the richest natural sources of vitamin C. It is added to oral beauty supplements and drinks as a plant-based vitamin C source.
The one controlled skin study found tested a multi-ingredient drink, so effects specific to acerola have not been separated out.
How it works: Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen synthesis and an antioxidant; acerola is used to supply it in a natural-sounding form.
Risks and caveats: The fruit is a food and no cosmetic-specific safety concerns are documented in the sources reviewed. The plant's leaves have stinging hairs that can irritate skin.
deepLead:
Acerola fruit extract is a preparation made from the fruit of Malpighia emarginata, a tropical shrub native to the Neotropics and grown commercially in Brazil and other warm regions. The raw fruit is among the richest natural sources of vitamin C, with one nutrition table listing roughly 1,678 mg per 100 g.
In skincare and beauty nutrition, acerola extract appears mainly as a natural vitamin C source in drinkable and oral supplements, often alongside collagen peptides, zinc, biotin and vitamin E. It is also used in the food industry, for example as a natural antioxidant in meat products.
Evidence for an appearance effect specific to acerola is limited. A randomized, placebo-controlled study tested a multi-ingredient drink that contained acerola extract together with collagen peptides and other nutrients in women aged 35 and older, but because the product was a blend, the contribution of acerola alone cannot be separated.

name: Orchid extract

angle.text: Orchid extracts from species such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis are used in Asian skincare, promoted as antioxidant and anti-aging botanicals. Support is limited to lab, animal and patent material.

summary: Antioxidant K-beauty botanical from several orchid species; support is limited to lab, animal and patent material.
note: Species vary widely and no human skin trial was found.
currentQuick:
Orchid extract is a botanical cosmetic ingredient, usually marketed as antioxidant and anti-aging. It is not a single substance: different orchid species are used.
Published work consists of cell and animal studies plus patents.
How it works: Proposed mechanisms are antioxidant activity and, in one cell model, reduced melanocyte precursor differentiation.
Risks and caveats: No safety data specific to cosmetic orchid extracts were found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Orchid extract refers to preparations from various orchid species used in cosmetics, most often marketed as antioxidant or anti-aging botanicals in Asian skincare. The orchid family (Orchidaceae) is very large, so the term covers different species, such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis, with different chemistry.
Published research on orchid extracts is mostly laboratory and animal work. Examples include a Phalaenopsis extract tested in a cell-culture model of sun-induced pigment spots and a Dendrobium extract tested in rats for bone loss. Patent filings describe Dendrobium chrysotoxum extract for anti-aging cosmetic use.
No human clinical trial of an orchid extract for skin appearance was found.

name: Lotus extract

angle.text: Sacred lotus extract is used in K-beauty skincare as an antioxidant botanical for a calmer, brighter complexion. Only two small human studies exist, both pairing it with green tea.

summary: Sacred-lotus botanical in K-beauty skincare; only two small human studies exist, both paired with green tea.
note: Do not confuse with blue lotus (Nymphaea), a different plant.
currentQuick:
Lotus extract comes from the sacred lotus and is used in skincare as an antioxidant ingredient.
Two small 2013 studies tested lotus combined with green tea on wrinkles and oiliness.
How it works: It is proposed to act through antioxidant flavonoids and related plant compounds.
Risks and caveats: No specific cosmetic safety problems were identified in the sources reviewed. Blue lotus extracts are a different product with their own safety assessment.
deepLead:
Lotus extract is derived from the sacred lotus (Nelumbo nucifera), an aquatic perennial whose seeds, rhizomes and leaves have long been used in food and in folk, Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine. It appears as an antioxidant botanical in K-beauty and other skincare products. The name is also applied to unrelated plants such as blue lotus (Nymphaea caerulea), which has different chemistry.
Human evidence is small. Two 2013 studies tested topical formulations of green tea and lotus extract on facial wrinkles and sebum in small groups of healthy adults. Other lotus research is in animals or the laboratory.

name: Green tea (Camellia sinensis) leaf extract

angle.text: Green tea extract is a common skincare antioxidant, also taken orally, used by people aiming for calmer, more youthful skin and fewer breakouts. It is widely studied for general health, with appearance-specific support more limited.

summary: Catechin-rich antioxidant botanical common in skincare; general health claims lack strong support and oral extracts carry liver warnings.
note: Oral extracts linked to liver toxicity; evidence here is from a single encyclopedia summary.
currentQuick:
Green tea extract concentrates the polyphenols of green tea leaf and is used in creams, serums and supplements as an antioxidant.
Reviews summarized on Wikipedia found insufficient evidence for most claims, though one topical form is an approved prescription for genital warts.
How it works: Catechins such as EGCG are antioxidants; no proven biological effects in humans are stated for them in the source.
Risks and caveats: Extracts, especially oral, have been linked to liver injury; EFSA could not set a safe dose. Rare skin reactions are reported.
deepLead:
Green tea leaf extract is a concentrate of polyphenols, mainly catechins such as epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), from unoxidized Camellia sinensis leaves. It is used in topical skincare as an antioxidant and in oral supplements.
Wikipedia reports that human clinical research has not found good evidence of benefit for most health claims, and that a 2011 European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) review judged most proposed claims, including some about skin protection from UV damage, not sufficiently supported. Oral extracts have been associated with liver toxicity, mainly attributed to EGCG, and Health Canada recommended warning labels in 2017.

name: Papaya extract

angle.text: Papaya extract is used as an enzyme exfoliant in masks and cleansers, promoted for smoother, brighter skin through papain's protein-digesting action. Skin-appearance trials for the extract were not found.

summary: Papaya-derived enzyme exfoliant botanical; no skin-appearance trials found and the FDA warned on topical papain drug products in 2008.
note: Possible allergy risk, particularly for people with latex allergy.
currentQuick:
Papaya extract is used in skincare mainly as an enzyme exfoliant because papaya latex contains papain, a protein-digesting enzyme.
No human trial for skin appearance was found; research is on other uses and in animals.
How it works: Papain breaks down proteins, which is the basis for exfoliation and wound-debridement uses.
Risks and caveats: The FDA warned in 2008 about topical papain drug products after hypersensitivity reports. People allergic to latex may also react to papaya.
deepLead:
Papaya extract is a preparation from the fruit, leaves, seeds or latex of Carica papaya. In skincare it is usually described as an enzyme exfoliant, because papaya latex is the source of the protein-digesting enzyme papain.
Papain is used in meat tenderizers, enzymatic wound debridement products and dental caries gels. No human trial of papaya extract for skin appearance was found; published research covers other uses, including a systematic review of papaya extract in dengue, and animal and in vitro studies.
In 2008 the US FDA warned companies to stop marketing topical papain drug products, citing reports of hypersensitivity reactions, and latex-allergic people may be at higher risk of reacting to papaya.

name: Oat extract

angle.text: Colloidal oat and oat extracts are used in sensitive-skin, baby and sun-care products to calm dry, irritated skin. Colloidal oatmeal holds FDA skin-protectant status, while trials of oat extracts for appearance are mostly dietary.

summary: Colloidal-oat soothing ingredient with FDA skin-protectant status; trials found for oat extracts are mostly dietary, not skin appearance.
note: Anti-itch and anti-inflammatory claims rest partly on non-primary sources.
currentQuick:
Oat extract in skincare is mostly colloidal oatmeal or avenanthramide-standardized extract, used to soothe dry or irritated skin.
The FDA is reported to have approved colloidal oatmeal as a skin protectant in 2003.
How it works: Avenanthramides are proposed to reduce inflammation, including through NF-kappaB inhibition, and to ease itch.
Risks and caveats: No safety data on cosmetic oat extract were available in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Oat extract in skincare usually means colloidal oatmeal or oat kernel extracts standardized for avenanthramides, phenolic compounds in Avena sativa that are studied as an anti-inflammatory component of oats. It is used in sensitive-skin, baby and sun-care products. The same name is also used for oat beta-glucan fiber extracts and green-oat extracts studied as foods or supplements, which are different preparations.
Wikipedia states that the US FDA approved colloidal oatmeal as a skin protectant in 2003. Oat baths were in use for itchy skin conditions in the 19th century and, according to the same source, earlier in antiquity.

name: Cucumber extract

angle.text: Cucumber extract is a cooling botanical in cleansers, gels and eye products, used for a fresh feel and a less puffy, tired-looking eye area. It is included more for mild hydration than as an active ingredient, with no controlled appearance trials.

summary: A cooling, hydrating botanical in cleansers and eye products; popular imagery, but no controlled evidence for appearance benefits.
note: Many "cucumber extract" papers are about sea cucumbers, a different organism.
currentQuick:
Cucumber extract is made from the fruit or seeds of the cucumber plant and appears in gels, toners and eye products as a cooling, soothing ingredient.
Its reputation rests largely on the fruit being mostly water and on the familiar image of cucumber slices on the eyes. Published research on skin outcomes is essentially absent.
How it works: Manufacturers describe it as hydrating and soothing. No studies in the sources reviewed have measured a specific mechanism on human skin.
Risks and caveats: Oral toxicity and mutagenicity studies of a standardized extract exist, but they concern ingestion. Topical risks are those of any plant-based cosmetic, mainly individual irritation or allergy to the finished product.
deepLead:
Cucumber extract is a preparation made from the fruit, and sometimes the seeds, of Cucumis sativus, an annual vine of the gourd family that has been cultivated for at least 3,000 years . In skincare it is listed as a cooling, soothing botanical, and it is usually included in cleansers, toners, gels and eye products for its fresh-feel and mild, hydrating character rather than as an active ingredient.
The raw fruit is about 95 percent water, which is the basis of its reputation as a hydrating, cooling ingredient . Published research on "cucumber extract" is sparse and mixed in topic: many indexed papers actually concern sea cucumbers, which are unrelated marine animals, and several others use cucumber extract as a laboratory reagent rather than as a skincare product .
For appearance use, no published human trial in the sources reviewed has shown that cucumber extract improves skin. A standardized cucumber extract has been assessed in oral toxicity and mutagenicity studies , and a small trial of cucumber seed extract for sun-induced redness is registered .

name: Chamomile extract

angle.text: Chamomile extract is a common soothing ingredient in creams, cleansers and masks, used by people with sensitive or red skin for a calmer look. Lab data on inflammation and oral-use trials exist, while skin-appearance trials do not.

summary: A calming flower extract in many soothing creams; lab data on inflammation and oral-use trials, but no skin-appearance trials.
note: Asteraceae allergy cross-reactivity is possible.
currentQuick:
Chamomile extract comes from daisy-like flowers and is a staple soothing ingredient in sensitive-skin products and herbal teas.
Research has mostly tested it by mouth for anxiety and sleep, or in cell and animal inflammation models. Studies of cosmetic skin outcomes are not found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Lab work reports that chamomile flavonoids and other constituents dampen inflammatory signaling, including the COX-2 pathway, in cultured cells.
Risks and caveats: People allergic to daisy-family plants such as ragweed or chrysanthemum may react. Oral use has cautions around anticoagulants and pregnancy.
deepLead:
Chamomile extract is prepared from the flower heads of daisy-like plants in the Asteraceae family, most often German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla) and Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile) . It is used in herbal teas and in cosmetics, where it is a common soothing or calming botanical in creams, cleansers and masks.
The flowers contain flavonoids and polyphenols such as apigenin, quercetin and luteolin, along with coumarins . Laboratory studies have reported that chamomile preparations inhibit inflammatory pathways in cultured cells, including COX-2 and prostaglandin release .
Human research has focused mainly on oral extracts for anxiety and sleep rather than on skin appearance . Wikipedia states that there is no clinical evidence chamomile treats any disease . No trial in the sources reviewed tests chamomile extract for a cosmetic skin outcome.

name: Pomegranate extract

angle.text: Pomegranate extract is taken orally or applied in skincare by people who want antioxidant support for a clearer, more even complexion. Its ellagitannin content is well studied in the lab, while effects on skin appearance in people have not been confirmed.

summary: An ellagitannin-rich antioxidant extract with plenty of lab data and no confirmed skin-appearance results.
note: Regulators have acted against unproven disease claims by a major juice marketer.
currentQuick:
Pomegranate extract concentrates the fruit's polyphenols, mainly ellagitannins, and is sold as a supplement and as an antioxidant ingredient in skincare.
Most research is in cells, rodents and metabolic studies in people. A trial on skin aging is registered, but no published skin-appearance result appears in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Ellagitannins are broken down by gut bacteria into urolithins, which are studied for anti-inflammatory activity. Anthocyanins and other polyphenols scavenge free radicals in lab assays.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed report no specific safety concerns with oral extract, but regulators have acted against unsupported health claims in marketing. Responses vary between people because gut microbiota differ.
deepLead:
Pomegranate extract is a concentrate of polyphenols obtained from the fruit, peel or seeds of Punica granatum, a tree native to the region spanning the Caucasus and the Iranian plateau . It is sold as an oral supplement and used in skincare as an antioxidant, with marketing built on its ellagitannin content.
The most abundant phytochemicals in the juice are ellagitannins, also called punicalagins, together with anthocyanins such as delphinidin and cyanidin . After ingestion, gut bacteria convert ellagitannins to urolithins, and people differ in which urolithin "metabotype" they produce .
Laboratory studies show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity . Wikipedia notes that research data are limited and that the US FDA and FTC have taken action over unproven health claims made by one major pomegranate juice marketer . A registered trial on skin aging and inflammation exists, but its results are not summarized in the sources reviewed .

name: Aloe leaf extract

angle.text: Aloe leaf extract is a staple of after-sun gels, moisturizers and facial products, used to soothe and hydrate skin so it looks calmer and smoother. Evidence on wound healing is mixed, and its effect on skin appearance specifically is lightly studied.

summary: The classic soothing plant gel in after-sun and moisturizers; widely used, with conflicting evidence on wounds and little on appearance.
note: Whole-leaf and latex products carry oral safety and regulatory concerns; the cosmetic limit on anthraquinones is 50 ppm.
currentQuick:
Aloe leaf extract comes from the succulent Aloe vera and is a standard soothing, moisturizing ingredient in lotions, after-sun products and cosmetics.
Wikipedia describes evidence for burns and wounds as conflicting. Small registered trials are mostly in oral and gum conditions, and none in the sources reviewed test cosmetic appearance.
How it works: The gel contains the polysaccharide acemannan and is mostly water; the laboratory studies reviewed report antibacterial and anti-tumor-promoting activity of aloe preparations.
Risks and caveats: Topical use is generally uncommon to cause problems, though allergy is possible. Oral latex or whole-leaf extract is linked to cramps, diarrhea and hepatitis, and regulators have acted on aloin laxatives and whole-leaf extract.
deepLead:
Aloe leaf extract is a preparation from the leaves of Aloe vera, a succulent plant long used on the skin, with records of use dating to the fourth millennium BCE . In cosmetics it is a common soothing and moisturizing ingredient in lotions, gels, sunscreens, shampoos and facial products .
The leaf yields two main materials. The clear inner gel contains the polysaccharide acemannan, while the yellow latex contains aloin, an anthraquinone with laxative properties that is considered toxic . The cosmetic industry limits anthraquinone content in aloe extracts to 50 parts per million .
Wikipedia describes the evidence for burns and wounds as conflicting, and says topical use in small amounts is likely safe with allergic reactions possible . Laboratory studies report antibacterial and anti-tumor-promoting activity of aloe preparations , and several small trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov test aloe gel in oral and gum conditions .

name: Sugarcane extract

angle.text: Sugarcane extract is promoted as a natural, gentle source of glycolic acid for exfoliating dull skin and smoothing texture. Glycolic acid itself is well studied as an exfoliant, while the plant extract has not been tested for skin results.

summary: A plant source of glycolic acid pitched as a gentle natural exfoliant; the AHA is well known, the extract itself is untested for skin.
note: Acid content of sugarcane extracts is unclear; AHAs can increase sun sensitivity.
currentQuick:
Sugarcane extract is used in skincare chiefly as a plant-derived source of glycolic acid, an alpha hydroxy acid that loosens surface skin cells.
Research on the extract itself is mostly in cells and animals, and no skin-appearance trial appears in the sources reviewed.
How it works: AHAs act as chemical exfoliants. Separately, polyphenol-rich sugarcane extract shows antioxidant and enzyme-inhibiting activity in lab studies.
Risks and caveats: AHAs commonly cause mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA has warned they can increase sunburn likelihood. One anticancer paper on the polyphenol extract was retracted.
deepLead:
Sugarcane extract refers to preparations from Saccharum officinarum used in cosmetics, most often described as a natural source of alpha hydroxy acids, chiefly glycolic acid. Glycolic acid can be isolated from sugarcane and is also found in sugar beets, pineapple, cantaloupe and unripe grapes .
Alpha hydroxy acids are used in cosmetics for chemical exfoliation, and glycolic acid is listed among keratolytic agents used for acne . The most common side effects of AHAs are mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA has warned that AHAs can raise the likelihood of sunburn, an effect described as reversible when use stops . Skin products labeled "sugarcane extract" vary in what they contain and at what strength.
Separate from cosmetics, a polyphenol-rich sugarcane extract (PRSE) has been studied in cells and animals for antioxidant, metabolic and antiviral effects . A 2021 anticancer paper on PRSE was retracted . No trial in the sources reviewed tests sugarcane extract for skin appearance.

name: Apple fruit water

angle.text: Apple fruit water appears in some creams as a mild source of fruit acids (AHAs) for gentle exfoliation and a fresher look. The evidence for this use is a single 2018 formulation study.

summary: A mild fruit-acid botanical water in some creams; one formulation study and little else.
note: Very thin evidence base; AHA-containing products can raise sun sensitivity.
currentQuick:
Apple fruit water is a water extract of apple used in cosmetics as a gentle source of fruit acids and polyphenols.
The sources reviewed contain only one cosmetic formulation study, so little can be said about its effects on appearance.
How it works: The studied extract contained about 3.5 percent alpha hydroxy acids, which act as chemical exfoliants, plus antioxidant polyphenols.
Risks and caveats: AHAs commonly cause mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA has warned they may increase sunburn likelihood.
deepLead:
Apple fruit water is a water-based extract of apple fruit used in cosmetics as a mild source of fruit acids and polyphenols. The sources reviewed contain a single dedicated study: a 2018 report on a cream containing 6 percent wild apple fruit water extract, said to contain 3.5 percent alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) along with polyphenolic compounds, stabilized with biodegradable alkyl-polyglucoside emulsifiers .
Alpha hydroxy acids are used in cosmetics for chemical exfoliation, with mild irritation, redness and flaking as the most common side effects, and the FDA has warned that they can increase the likelihood of sunburn . Beyond this one cosmetic formulation paper, little published research on apple fruit water as a skincare ingredient was found.

name: Turmeric root extract

angle.text: Turmeric root extract is used in skincare as a brightening and antioxidant ingredient, with users hoping for a more even, glowing complexion. Support for this use comes mainly from cell studies, with little human skin data.

summary: Curcumin-rich plant extract sold as a skin brightener; evidence for that use is limited to cell studies.
note: Contact allergen; strongly pigmented and can stain.
currentQuick:
Turmeric root extract comes from the Curcuma longa rhizome and is used in cosmetics as a brightening and antioxidant ingredient. Its main pigment is curcumin.
The sources reviewed here contain no human trials of topical turmeric extract for skin tone. Research is limited to cell-culture experiments.
How it works: In laboratory cell models curcumin has been reported to dampen TGF-beta signaling and, combined with another antioxidant, to reduce UV-induced oxidative damage in keratinocytes. Whether this translates to visible brightening in people has not been tested in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Curcumin is listed as a contact allergen and a strong yellow pigment. Oral use has been linked to side effects such as nausea and, rarely, liver injury, and a case report describes yellow discoloration of the feet. It is an approved food coloring in the US and E100 in the EU.
deepLead:
Turmeric root extract is a preparation made from the rhizome of Curcuma longa, a plant of the ginger family. Its main colored constituent is curcumin, a yellow polyphenol that is also used as a food coloring, a dietary supplement ingredient and a cosmetic ingredient. In skincare it is marketed mainly as a brightening or antioxidant ingredient.
Laboratory work has examined curcumin and turmeric extract in skin-cell models, for example a 2023 cell-culture study combining turmeric root extract with another antioxidant in keratinocytes exposed to ultraviolet light. No clinical trial of topical turmeric root extract for skin brightening or complexion appears among the sources reviewed for this entry. Wikipedia's curcumin article states that extensive studies have not established medical value for curcumin, citing its instability and poor absorption, and also lists it as a contact allergen.

name: Menthyl lactate

angle.text: Menthyl lactate is a milder, longer-lasting cooling agent used in cosmetics, fragrances and oral-care products to give a fresh sensation. It is valued for feel in products, and no study has tested it for changes in how skin looks.

summary: Menthol-derived cooling ingredient used for feel in cosmetics; no evidence it changes appearance.
note: Little published research; sensorial rather than cosmetic-effect ingredient.
currentQuick:
Menthyl lactate is a menthol-lactic acid ester used to give products a cooling feel. It appears in cosmetics, fragrances, oral care and some tobacco products.
No published study in the sources reviewed tests it for any appearance outcome.
How it works: Patents describe it as a physiological coolant that produces a cooling sensation, with properties compared to menthol.
Risks and caveats: The main safety document in the sources is a RIFM fragrance-ingredient assessment. Little other safety literature on skincare use was found.
deepLead:
Menthyl lactate is an ester of menthol and lactic acid used as a cooling agent, giving a milder and longer-lasting cooling sensation than menthol in product formulations described in patents. It appears in cosmetics, fragrances, oral-care and tobacco products.
It is relevant to skincare mainly as a sensorial ingredient (a cooling or soothing feel) rather than as an agent with a documented effect on appearance. Published literature on it is sparse: the sources reviewed consist of a fragrance safety assessment, a study of coolants in tobacco, patents and an unrelated conservation-science preprint.

name: Exosome serums

angle.text: Exosome serums are promoted for skin regeneration and rejuvenation, often applied after microneedling to speed recovery and improve texture. The biology is promising in the lab, while published human skin data remain very limited.

summary: Vesicle-based regeneration serums with promising biology but almost no published human skin data.
note: Product composition is hard to standardize; no published efficacy results found.
currentQuick:
Exosome serums contain extracellular vesicles, tiny particles cells release to signal each other, and are marketed for skin regeneration, often with microneedling.
Only a couple of registered trials turned up, and no published results for cosmetic use.
How it works: Vesicles carry proteins, lipids and RNA between cells; the idea behind the products is that these signals could influence skin cells. This has not been shown for the products in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Vesicle science has persistent standardization and contamination problems. No regulatory or adverse-event data for cosmetic products were in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Exosome serums are skincare and post-procedure products marketed as containing exosomes or other extracellular vesicles, small membrane-enclosed particles that cells release. They are promoted for regeneration and rejuvenation, often alongside procedures such as microneedling.
Extracellular vesicles are an active research area, but in the sources reviewed the evidence for cosmetic products is limited to a small number of registered trials. Researchers have noted that isolating and measuring vesicles is difficult and standardization is lacking.

name: Mesenchymal stem cell conditioned media

angle.text: Stem-cell conditioned media appear in serums and post-procedure treatments marketed for skin regeneration and rejuvenation. The idea draws on lab findings about the growth factors they contain, and human evidence so far is limited to early-phase trials.

summary: Stem-cell secretome liquid sold for regeneration; lab promise, only early-phase human trials.
note: Secreted factors can have effects beyond repair in lab studies; no cosmetic efficacy trials found.
currentQuick:
MSC conditioned media is the nutrient liquid in which stem cells have grown, containing the growth factors and vesicles they secrete. It is used in serums and post-procedure treatments as a cell-free regenerative ingredient.
Most evidence is lab and animal wound-healing work; human trials are small and early-phase.
How it works: The secreted proteins, growth factors and vesicles are thought to signal to nearby cells, for example promoting fibroblast migration and dampening inflammation in cell models.
Risks and caveats: Composition varies between preparations. A laboratory study reported MSC-derived chemokines promoting tumor-cell invasion, and no long-term cosmetic safety data were found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Mesenchymal stem cell conditioned media (MSC-CM), also called the MSC secretome, is the liquid in which mesenchymal stem cells have been grown, containing the proteins, growth factors, vesicles and other molecules they release. Versions made from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-CM) are among those studied. Products based on it are marketed in serums and post-procedure treatments for regeneration.
Most of the published research is laboratory or animal work on wound healing and inflammation, and reviews describe it as a possible cell-free alternative to stem cell therapy. Early-phase human trials are registered for conditions such as chronic ulcers and keloids; the sources reviewed here do not report their results.

name: Fibroblast growth factor (FGF)

angle.text: Topical FGF is added to some anti-aging serums on the strength of its role in wound repair, with the aim of firmer, smoother-looking skin. It is well studied in wound healing, and human cosmetic trials for wrinkles were not found.

summary: Wound-healing growth factor put in anti-aging serums, with no human cosmetic trials found.
note: Overactive FGF signaling is linked to disease; no cosmetic safety data found.
currentQuick:
FGFs are a family of signaling proteins that drive cell growth and wound repair. FGF2 (bFGF) is the form most often discussed for skin, and some anti-aging serums contain growth factors of this type.
No trials of topical FGF serums for aging skin were found.
How it works: FGFs bind receptors on cells and promote fibroblast proliferation, blood vessel formation and granulation tissue in wound healing.
Risks and caveats: Overactive FGF signaling is associated with several diseases. Safety of cosmetic use was not covered in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) are a family of 23 signaling proteins in humans that regulate cell growth, tissue organization and wound healing, signaling through four receptor types (FGFR1-4). FGF2, also called basic FGF (bFGF), promotes blood vessel formation, fibroblast proliferation and granulation tissue in wound repair. Topical FGF is included in some anti-aging serums.
Wikipedia states that FGF2 has been shown to enhance tissue repair in clinical settings such as burns, skin grafts and ulcers, and lists trafermin, a recombinant FGF2 drug, among FGF receptor agonists. The sources reviewed contain no trials of topical FGF serums for wrinkles or skin aging.

name: Anagain

angle.text: Anagain is a pea-sprout cosmetic ingredient in hair-growth serums, discussed alongside Redensyl, Capixyl and Baicapil by people seeking fuller hair. Support is a small 10-person gene-expression study.

summary: Pea-sprout extract sold in cosmetic hair serums; backed by one tiny 10-person gene-expression study.
note: Evidence limited to a very small, short study of gene expression.
currentQuick:
Anagain is a branded extract from pea sprouts used in over-the-counter hair serums. It is promoted as a topical hair-growth active.
Published evidence consists of a small study of 10 volunteers measuring gene expression after applying a 2% extract, and a review that lists it among hyped cosmeceutical actives.
How it works: Manufacturers and the one small study describe an effect on expression of genes involved in hair growth; this has not been shown to translate into measured hair-count outcomes in large trials.
Risks and caveats: No safety problems were identified in the sources reviewed, but no large safety data exist. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved hair-loss drug.
deepLead:
Anagain (also written AnaGain) is a cosmetic hair-care ingredient derived from the sprouts of the pea plant, marketed in topical hair-growth serums and lotions. It is a branded cosmetic active rather than a drug, and it is discussed in appearance communities alongside other 'hair-growth actives' such as Redensyl, Capixyl and Baicapil.
Published human evidence is limited to small, short studies. A short communication in Phytotherapy Research reported that a fluid containing 2% pea sprout extract applied to a defined scalp zone in 10 volunteers changed the expression of genes relevant to hair growth. A 2025 review of cosmeceutical hair-loss actives lists AnaGain among the ingredients it examines, noting that such products are heavily promoted on social media.
